articles.title: DFA: EU privacy rules limit info on Zaldy Co, Harry Roque asylum cases
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Friday said strict privacy rules in Europe limit its ability to obtain information about the asylum cases of former lawmaker Zaldy Co and former…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 11:26pm

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Friday said strict privacy rules in Europe limit its ability to obtain information about the asylum cases of former lawmaker Zaldy Co and former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque.

Co faces graft, plunder, and malversation charges over alleged irregularities in government flood control projects, while Roque faces qualified human trafficking charges linked to the Lucky South 99 POGO hub in Porac, Pampanga. Both have reportedly sought asylum in Europe.

“Mr. Chair, ang European Union, France included, have very strict privacy [rules]. So kung nag-file man po siya [Zaldy Co] ng asylum, hindi tayo bibigyan ng information because this is their law, this is their regulation. So yun po ang status. So maski na po anong tanong ng ating embahada, hindi po tayo bibigyan ng impormasyon,” DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said during the agency’s budget hearing at the Senate.

(Mr. Chair, the European Union, France included, have very strict privacy rules. So if he filed for asylum, we will not be given information because this is their law, this is their regulation. So that is the status. Even if our embassy asks, we will not be given information.)
The same restriction applies to Roque’s asylum case in Austria, which is also a member of the EU, Lazaro said.
Citing the Philippine Embassy in Vienna, Lazaro said there was no information confirming that Roque’s asylum application had been denied.
Lazaro also said the DFA would no longer issue passports to individuals subject to an arrest warrant. The passports of both Co and Roque have already been canceled, according to the DFA.
If they are returned to the Philippines, Lazaro said they would instead be issued one-way travel documents. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
articles.summary: Buffett's son, Howard, will succeed him in the role. Buffett had earlier stepped down as Berkshire's CEO last year.

image.caption: Buffett, the son of a US congressman, became interested in business and investing at a young age [FILE: May 5, 2019]Image: Nati Harnik/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Billionaire investor and philanthropist Warren Buffett is stepping down as the chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, the holding company said Friday.
Buffett is 96 years old. His son, 71-year-old Howard Buffett, will succeed him in the role as chairman.
'I have never felt better about what comes next'

"I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett told shareholders in a message. "Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world. This is not something many people my age can say, and I have never felt better about what comes next."
This comes after Buffett stepped down as the firm's CEO last year, with Greg Abel succeeding him in that position.

"Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values — both worth more than anything on our balance sheet," Buffett said. "Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against."
In a statement of his own, Abel said "the culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian."
How did Buffett lead Berkshire Hathaway?

Buffett purchased textile firm Berkshire Hathaway in 1965 and transformed it into a multinational conglomerate holding company with a worth of over $1 trillion (€871 billion) in terms of market capitalization. Most of the companies worth more than $1 trillion are in the tech sector.

blocks.caption: Warren Buffett (left in photo) was known for his partnership with the late Charlie Munger (right in photo) who had served as Berkshire's vice chairman [FILE: May 3, 2019]Image: Johannes Eisele/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Buffett's investment prowess has led to Berkshire beating the S&P market index in 40 out of the past 60 years.

Berkshire owns whole businesses in sectors such as insurance and energy; the firm also owns restaurant chain Dairy Queen. Moreover, Berkshire invests in companies such as Apple, Coca-Cola, Chevron and Bank of America.
According to Forbes, Buffett is the 10th-richest person in the world today with a net worth of $144.7 billion.

Buffett grew up in Omaha, Nebraska, where Berkshire is also headquartered. Known as the "Oracle of Omaha," Buffett has embraced a folksy public persona and is enamored with American staples such as McDonald's breakfasts, Dairy Queen sundaes and Coca Cola.

articles.title: NBI, BI investigate personnel linked to illegal recruitment flights
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and the Bureau of Immigration (BI) continue to deepen their parallel investigations into the facilitation of illegal recruitment flights by their own…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 11:11pm

The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and the Bureau of Immigration (BI) continue to deepen their parallel investigations into the facilitation of illegal recruitment flights by their own officers.

In a "24 Oras" report by John Consulta on Friday, the agencies’ probes continue following the arrest of an NBI agent facilitating the flight of an illegal recruit through a modus operandi similar to the "pastillas" scheme.

According to the BI, questions arose over how the passenger involved obtained a boarding pass nine hours before the scheduled flight, when standard practice dictates issuing passes only three hours prior to departure.

“Very much coordinated po ‘yung nangyaring pagpapadaan sa kaniya, pag-clear sa kaniya. Itinapat talaga doon sa oras ng shift nung officer who was supposed to clear her for departure,” BI Spokesperson Atty. Anisha Hassan said.
(Her passage and clearance were very much coordinated. It was timed specifically during the shift of the officer who was supposed to clear her for departure.)

“Nung nakita po natin ‘yung boarding pass niya, she was supposed to board the gate ng 9 a.m. because that is the time of [her] flight. Ang ipinagtataka po natin, ang usual po na practice at ang standard talaga three hours before pa lang, na-iisyuhan ng boarding pass ang lahat ng passengers. So tinitignan po natin yon as point of investigation,” she added.

(When we saw her boarding pass, she was supposed to board the gate at 9 a.m. because that was her flight time. What puzzles us is that standard practice dictates issuing boarding passes to passengers only three hours before the flight. So we are looking at that as a key point in the investigation.)
The BI said the Intelligence Officer I who facilitated the recruit's passage has been relieved of duty, while additional BI personnel remain under investigation.
Hassan stated that the relieved officer reportedly worked with two accomplices.

“By the order of the Commissioner, ito pong isa na organic personnel has been ordered into a floating status po and ‘yun pong job order personnel naman, immediately terminated for service,” she added.
(By order of the Commissioner, this organic personnel has been placed on floating status, while the job order personnel was immediately terminated from service.)
The NBI explained that the group operates with dedicated recruiters, human resource handlers, briefers, and "canners" to traffic recruits out of the country.

“May naka-task naman na mag-book ng flight niya, siya ‘yung gagawa ng kanyang itinerary kung saan papunta. At meron ding magbi-brief, ‘yung magsasabi kung paano ’yung gagawin, may step-by-step na gagawin,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag explained.
(Someone is tasked with booking the flight and creating the itinerary for the destination. Another person serves as the briefer to instruct the victim on the step-by-step procedure.)
“May tinatawag na gunner. Ito ngayon yung nahuli natin. ‘Yung canner na tinatawag, ito yung immigration officer kung saan dadaan ‘yung victims ng human trafficking para makalusot,” Matibag added.
(Then there is the so-called 'gunner.' This is the person we caught—the immigration officer through whom human trafficking victims pass to sneak through inspection.)
Authorities intercepted two Filipinos facilitated by the immigration officer, stopping one prior to aircraft boarding and securing the second at a Malaysian airport.

“Nakipag-coordinate tayo sa authorities ng Malaysia at madali naman silang nagresponde doon sa ating request at na-intercept po ang ating isang kababayan doon sa Malaysia,” NBI Human Trafficking Division Chief Agent Sally Laguardia said.
(We coordinated with Malaysian authorities, who responded quickly to our request, leading to the interception of our fellow citizen in Malaysia.) —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Ever more Israelis moving to and investing in Cyprus
articles.summary: Over the past three years, more and more Israelis have been purchasing property and investing in Cyprus, with many moving to the island permanently. How has this changed the Cypriot economy and how…

image.caption: The Israeli community in Cyprus is growing, as is the infrastructure catering to itImage: Loucianos Lyritsas/DW

blocks.text: The volatile situation in Israel and the prolonged sense of insecurity following the October 7, 2023 attacks and the wars that followed have prompted a growing number of Israelis to turn to the Republic of Cyprus.

For many, the nearby island is evolving from a holiday and investment destination into a place to settle permanently — and, in some cases, a "Plan B" in the event of a deterioration of the situation in Israel.
That is precisely how several Israelis who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity described their decision.
"I want to have a Plan B in case the situation in Israel gets more difficult," said one Israeli who recently bought a home in a large residential development in Cyprus's Limassol district.
Another pointed to Cyprus's proximity and familiarity: "It's a 40-minute flight, the same landscape, the same climate. It's like being in Israel without actually being there."
A third linked his move to business, saying that many Israeli companies have transferred some of their operations to Cyprus, making it easier for them to do business with EU countries.
First and second homes
The population of the Republic of Cyprus is less than a million.
According to estimates cited by Israeli media, at least 3,000 Israeli families now live permanently in Cyprus, with their number increasing by several hundred each year.

Israeli media reports also speak of tens of thousands of Israelis who have purchased property on the island. The newspaper Israel Hayom has reported that around 20,000 Israelis own property in Cyprus without living there year-round.

Figures from the Cyprus Land Registry presented to parliament show that between 2021 and 2024, a total of 3,851 property transfers and sale contracts involving Israeli buyers were recorded in the coastal districts of Larnaca, Paphos and Limassol alone.
Israeli-backed developments
But Israeli interest in Cyprus extends beyond apartments and holiday homes to land, tourism developments and major investment projects.

One of the most prominent examples is the Israeli hotel group Fattal, whose investments in Cyprus are estimated to run into hundreds of millions of euros and include hotels in Limassol, Paphos and Larnaca.

blocks.caption: A major Israeli-backed hotel development is underway in the Paphos district, just a few kilometers from the Akamas peninsula and its protected natural areaImage: Loucianos Lyritsas/DW

blocks.text: In Larnaca, investors with Israeli interests are also behind the redevelopment of the historic Palm Beach hotel, an investment of more than €110 million ($126 million), as well as the roughly €40 million Aqua Residences project, which foresees the construction of two 15-story towers along the seafront.

In the Limassol district, an Israeli investor is planning to revive Trozena, a village that has been abandoned for decades, by restoring around 60 homes and developing tourism facilities, a campsite and a winery.

The project, located within a Natura 2000 protected area, has sparked opposition and an investigation by the relevant authorities after some work began without the required planning and building permits.
Signs of a more permanent presence
At the same time, infrastructure catering to the Israeli community is becoming increasingly visible.
Places of worship, businesses and services for Israelis — such as restaurants offering kosher dining — have opened in Larnaca, Limassol and Paphos.

Hebrew-language advertisements can also be seen along the roads — including political campaign material. Last summer, billboards for Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party targeting Israeli voters appeared along Cypriot highways.

blocks.caption: In the summer, billboards for Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party targeting Israeli voters appeared on roadsides in CyprusImage: Loucianos Lyritsas/DW

blocks.text: Perhaps the clearest indication of the increasingly permanent nature of the Israeli presence is a planned private Jewish school in Polemidia, near Limassol, for up to 1,500 students.
Reminiscent of the influx of Russian capital after 2013
All of this has added momentum to an increasingly heated political debate over foreign investment and property ownership in general.

The debate is further shaped by what critics describe as Cyprus's unconditional diplomatic support for Israel and by the island's previous experience with the massive influx of Russian capital, which accelerated after Cyprus expanded its citizenship-by-investment program following the 2013 financial crisis.

Some of the strongest political criticism has come from Stefanos Stefanou, secretary general of Cyprus's Progressive Party of Working People (AKEL), and Fidias Panayiotou, MEP and leader of the Direct Democracy party.

AKEL is Cyprus's main left-wing party, and currently in the opposition. Stefanou warned of uncontrolled sales of Cypriot land to foreigners, specifically referring to purchases by Israelis and what he described as the creation of gated residential communities with their own infrastructure.

blocks.caption: Politician Stefanos Stefanou has warned of uncontrolled sales of Cypriot land to foreignersImage: Kostas Pikoulas/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Panayiotou went further, claiming that "Israel is buying Cyprus" and warning that the Cypriot economy risks becoming overly dependent on Israeli capital.
The remarks prompted a strong response from the Israeli side.

Israel's ambassador to Cyprus, Oren Anolik, rejected claims of excessive Israeli influence, arguing that the thousands of Israelis living and doing business on the island have become part of its social and economic fabric.
He also warned that singling out a particular nationality and invoking stereotypes about "foreign economic power" could fuel antisemitism.
Government keen to attract foreign investment

The Cypriot government has made attracting foreign investment a key economic priority, with President Nikos Christodoulides repeatedly stressing the goal of establishing Cyprus as an attractive destination for international investors.
When it comes specifically to Israeli investment, a statement by former Energy and Commerce Minister George Papanastasiou is indicative of the government's approach.

Speaking in 2025, while still in office, Papanastasiou said the government was "pleased to note that Israeli businesspeople are present in many sectors of the Cypriot economy," including tourism, technology, energy, health and real estate.
Debate in parliament
The debate has now reached parliament and has broadened to encompass property purchases by third-country nationals in general.

Lawmakers are considering legislative proposals from the country's two major parties, the left-wing AKEL and the center-right Democratic Rally (DISY), aimed at imposing restrictions on land purchases by non-EU nationals.

blocks.caption: Fidias Panayiotou, MEP and leader of the Direct Democracy party, has claimed that 'Israel is buying Cyprus' and warned that the Cypriot economy risks becoming overly dependent on Israeli capitalImage: Petros Karadjias/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: One of the proposals was submitted by DISY MP Nikos Georgiou. Speaking to DW, he said that "in recent years, land purchases by foreign nationals have reached unprecedented proportions," affecting "the demographic composition, land values and, in some cases, national security."

Georgiou stressed that his proposal "is not directed against any country or its citizens," adding that the debate should take place "without scaremongering, without rhetoric directed against citizens of any third country."

AKEL has submitted a similar legislative proposal. Speaking to DW, AKEL MP Giorgos Koukoumas said his party had raised the issue of mass and uncontrolled property purchases by foreign nationals because they are "one of the factors driving property prices to such levels that it becomes impossible for the average Cypriot to buy or even rent a home in the country's urban centers."
He also referred to concerns among what he says is a significant section of Cypriot society, specifically regarding purchases by Israelis.

These concerns, he said, "obviously have to do with the reality of sweeping acquisitions of major business enterprises and large areas of land by Israelis, the successive Israeli media reports speaking of the creation of a 'second Israel in Cyprus,' combined with the Israeli intelligence presence on our island and the relations with Israel in the fields of defense and security that have been promoted by the Cypriot government in recent years."

articles.title: Alleged underworld supporters and unfounded health claims: One Nation rolls out more Victorian election candidates
articles.summary:
Party has unveiled a steady stream of contenders for state election, including a former councillor who lost his licence for drink-driving

  • Get our

blocks.text: Candidates contesting the Victorian state election for One Nation include a former Liberal who has won support from alleged underworld figures, a naturopath who has endorsed Donald Trump’s unfounded claim that paracetamol is linked to autism and a former shire councillor who lost his licence for drink-driving.

Pauline Hanson announced who would be her party’s upper house candidates and Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, at a press conference last month. Since then One Nation has used social media to unveil a steady stream of candidates, with 51 of the 88 lower house spots now filled.
Among them is Michael Piastrino, who launched his campaign on Sunday for the outer-suburban seat of Berwick, held by the Liberal Brad Battin on a 4.7% margin.

blocks.caption: A selfie from Michael Piastrino’s Instagram account that shows Malaki Salesui standing behind him

blocks.text: The launch was attended by Malaki Salesui, who was convicted in 2021 for his role in an organised car-theft ring.

Mick Mantzaris commented on photographs of the event on Instagram, writing: “great day great people” and “time for a change”. Mantzaris pleaded guilty in 2012 to possessing testosterone, disclosing restricted information and misleading the office of police integrity. The following year he was targeted in a drive-by shooting. Police described him at the time as “an associate of some outlaw motorcycle gang members”.

Anthony Younan, the nephew of the slain underworld figure Nabil Maghnie, also commented on Piastrino’s Instagram posts, saying he would vote for One Nation because of him: “I can’t believe I am going to vote for a red headed woman who hate Arabs. My mother is going to disown me Michael. But I am doing this for you bro!”

blocks.caption: Anthony Younan’s comment on a Piastrino post

blocks.text: Piastrino, a hairdresser, ran for the Liberals at the 2022 election. He was forced to apologise during that campaign after declaring that Daniel Andrews would be “brought to justice for the murder of 800 people” under a Liberal government.
He told the Cranbourne Star News last month that he had met Mantzaris and Salesui through church. “I’m not here to judge people,” he said. “I’m here to help people.”

Sources have told Guardian Australia that One Nation has strengthened its candidate vetting process in the lead-up to the November election, with more stringent background checks and lengthy interviews.

In an interview in June, Kelvin Morton, One Nation’s general manager, said the party had also employed technology that did a “very comprehensive deep dive” into potential candidates’ social media accounts and provided a “thorough assessment” of their characters.
One Nation also shown a willingness to accept candidates with controversial histories, including Pickering, who this month acknowledged past drug use and drink-driving.
Ben Lucas, the party’s candidate for the Liberal-held seat of Narracan, resigned from Baw Baw shire council in 2021 after being convicted of drink-driving and dangerous driving.
Court records seen by Guardian Australia show he was fined $2,000 and had his licence suspended for two years.
This month he pleaded guilty to operating a category-one aquatic facility without registering it with the council and was ordered to pay $3,000 in costs.

Lucas described the charges, which related to the operation of ice baths at his gym, on Facebook as a “storm in a teacup” that had been “blown out of proportion”. He said they arose from an “administrative oversight” involving the registration of his business after it moved.
“If I wasn’t involved with One Nation, would this have still been pursued in the same way?” he wrote.
after newsletter promotion

Several One Nation candidates have deleted or scrubbed their social media accounts since announcing their candidacies, including Elita Dabrowski, who is contesting Sunbury, a seat Labor fears it could lose.
A deleted tweet, seen by Guardian Australia, shows Dabrowski backed Trump’s claim that paracetamol is linked to autism.

“This morning I watched Trump’s announcement on autism, vaccination schedules & paracetamol,” she wrote on 23 September 2025. “As a naturopath & functional health practitioner, I felt proud – it reflects what I see in clinic every day.”
Trump had said pregnant women should limit their use of the medication, claiming it heightens the risk of autism in children – an assertion disputed by scientists.
Meanwhile, Tammy Lindrum, One Nation’s candidate for the historically safe Labor seat of Albert Park, has left a trail of comments on Meta’s Threads about Muslim and First Nations people.

Under the handle “Lindrum Legends” and the username Tam Lindrum, she responded in April 2025 to a since-deleted post, saying there was “Black and Muslim supremacy in Australia” and that “the Whitman [sic] can’t say anything as they risk being accused of being racist”. Three months later, responding to another post, she wrote: “If you don’t like Bacon go back to a Muslim country.”
Responding to a post about plans to make the First Peoples’ Assembly of Victoria permanent, she wrote: “For a minority group I think we are going a little too far.
“We have paid their housing, welfare, education, health, for many years. When does that stop?”
Among candidates announced this week is Bruce Whalley, who blamed children for the climate crisis in tweet posted during the 2019 student strikes for climate action.

“Climate change is the fault of kids,” he wrote. “Stop asking for a car lift to school. WALK! RIDE a BIKE! or CATCH PUBLIC TRANSPORT. Gosh! Start to be a generation of doers Not talkers and complainers.”

Whalley, who is running in Labor-held Bundoora, also describes himself on Instagram as an “ABC2 TV Think Tank tragic” – despite One Nation’s plan to defund the broadcaster, and its ban on its journalists attending the party’s media events.

articles.title: Swedish teenager jailed for attempted murder, rape and assault committed online, with victims in Germany and Australia
articles.summary:
Eighteen-year-old known as Chai was active in networks notorious for their sadistic exploitation of young people

A Swedish teenager known as Chai has been sentenced to more than 10 years in…

blocks.text: A Swedish teenager known as Chai has been sentenced to more than 10 years in jail for attempted murder, rape and aggravated assault – crimes committed via the internet, including against a teenage girl in Australia.

The district court found that Chai, 18, was active in online networks notorious for their sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people, coercing them to create sexually explicit material or engage in acts of violence – and for the youth of those involved.
The teenager was between 15 and 17 when the offences were committed.
Chai was convicted of two counts of attempted murder against a young person in Germany, and multiple sexual and violent offences against the Australian teenager, among other offences.

Jenny Östling, a senior public prosecutor at Sweden’s national unit against international and organised crime, said the court had clearly understood the phenomenon of “nihilistic violent extremism” and the Com – an umbrella term for a loosely connected online network that engages in cybercrime, extortion and violence.
“I’m really glad that they realise how serious this is and what it is,” she said.

She noted that the sentence was among the longest possible in Sweden for someone of Chai’s age. The court also found that it was possible for someone to be convicted of violent offences even where they were committed remotely via the internet.
“That is a very important tool for us when we proceed [with] these kinds of cases,” Östling said.

The crimes committed by those involved with sadistic extortion networks, such as one globally known as “764”, often cross borders, with cases in the US, the UK, Germany and Australia, and alleged victims in multiple jurisdictions.

Material is often created and traded among participants to build status and control, lawyers and researchers told the Guardian as part of its investigation into these groups, as well as a means of accessing closed servers and chatrooms.
“These are young people recruiting other young people,” Bjørn Ihler, the founder of the security firm Revontulet, said at the time. “It is a youth phenomenon.”

Chai’s conviction is one of several cases that have resulted in significant terms of imprisonment for young men found to be involved in this ecosystem, including an American, Kyle Spitze, 27, who was sentenced in August to 77 years in prison – the longest federal sentence yet imposed on someone the US government has labelled a “nihilistic violent extremist”.
During the trial, Chai underwent a forensic psychiatric examination that found he was not suffering a serious mental disorder when the offences occurred.
His lawyer, Emily Tovedal, told the Guardian: “The defence’s view is that the court has made an error of judgment regarding a large proportion of the charges.”
Authorities internationally have increasingly raised the alarm about sadistic online exploitation of young people, detailing potential warning signs including self-harm and isolation.
“Sadly, I’m confident that … they will probably grow,” Östling said of these networks. “And we will also be aware of more of them, because now we know what to look for.”

articles.title: Marcos orders thorough probe into Banga High School shooting
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. ordered concerned government agencies to conduct a thorough investigation into the school shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato that left…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 10:44pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. ordered concerned government agencies to conduct a thorough investigation into the school shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato that left three students dead and several others injured.
In a statement, Marcos expressed his sympathies to the families who lost their children in the shooting and assured them they would receive the necessary assistance.

“Ngayon, iniutos ko sa Department of Education, DILG (Department of the Interior and Local Government), at Philippine National Police na mag-report sa akin ukol sa mga hakbang na naisagawa na matapos ang mga nakaraang insidente. Sa mga susunod na araw, ilalabas natin ang karagdagang mga hakbang upang tugunan ang mga puwang na nananatili at mas mapangalagaan ang ating mga mag-aaral,” Marcos said.

(Today, I ordered the Department of Education, DILG, and the Philippine National Police to report to me on the steps taken following previous incidents. In the coming days, we will announce additional measures to address the remaining gaps and better protect our students.)
“Iniutos ko rin ang isang masusing imbestigasyon sa naganap na pamamaril ngayong araw, kabilang na kung paano nakakuha at nakapasok ang isang menor de edad ng baril sa loob ng paaralan,” he added.
(I also ordered a thorough investigation into today’s shooting, including how a minor obtained a gun and brought it into the school.)
Marcos also ordered concerned agencies to strengthen security measures in schools.
“Hindi natin maaaring tanggapin na maging bahagi na lamang ng buhay ng ating mga anak ang mga pamamaril sa paaralan,” Marcos said.
(We cannot allow school shootings to become a part of our children’s lives.)
Children have the right to study without fear, while parents have the right to send their children to school knowing they are safe, Marcos said.

The South Cotabato shooting was the country’s third school shooting since June. A shooting at a school in Tacloban City in June left three people dead, while a shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga in August left two students dead, including the shooter. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Canada and EU: A look at the bloc's special relationships
articles.summary: Though Canada may be some distance from Europe geographically, closer political ties are in the cards. With talk of an associate membership, DW takes a look at other arrangements the EU has with…

image.caption: Mark Carney sees Canada and the EU as a natural partnershipImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Canada and the EU "see the world with the same eyes," according to European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
And the feeling appears mutual.

"Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

In that spirit, and with both parties grasping for an effective way to deal with Donald Trump and his tariffs, von der Leyen floated the idea that Canada could become the European Union's first associate member on Thursday.

Given the concept of associate membership does not yet exist, it's difficult to determine exactly what that would mean. Germany proposed a similar arrangement for Ukraine earlier this year, only for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to reject the idea on the grounds that the country wants full membership.
Though not officially recognized as associates, there are plenty of countries that have strong ties or agreements with the bloc. DW looks at some of them and how they work.
EFTA and single market access — Norway, Liechtenstein, Iceland

Under this model, the ‘European Free Trade Association (EFTA)' countries are part of the EU's internal market, so people, goods and services can move freely in the Schengen area. The three countries also follow many EU rules in areas like tourism, environment and education.

But there are some key distinctions. The countries have no part in the decision-making process, bar some input into policy preparation, such as participation in expert groups. They are also not in the customs union, do not use the Euro and are not bound by the EU's common trade policy or justice laws. Iceland held a referendum on whether to go for full membership last month, but the government's push to do so failed and they remain an EFTA country.
Bilateral agreements — Switzerland

While it borders four EU member states (Germany, Italy, France and Austria), Switzerland has never been a full member. Instead, more than 120 bilateral deals have been agreed upon by the EU and Switzerland over the last 50 years. These relate to areas such as trade, transport, security and education. A new package of deals was finalized last year, 20 years after they were last agreed.
As Trump menaces, some think Canada should join the EU

More than 1.5 million EU citizens live and work in Switzerland, while 466,200 Swiss have gone the other way. That is possible as Switzerland is also part of theSchengen area, allowing for free movement of people across borders.

Switzerland makes financial contributions to a number of EU member states that joined after expansion in 2004, mostly in the east of Europe, but it has no EU voting rights and adopts only some EU laws. Switzerland can also participate in certain EU programs and research projects, through individual negotiations.
The post Brexit agreement — UK

More than four years after the UK voted to leave the EU in a 2016 referendum, the two parties signed a trade and cooperation agreement. Negotiations were fraught and complex, and the UK now has limited access to the EU market and is aligned with the EU on some areas of policy and regulation, for now at least.

There is no longer free movement of people from the UK to the EU or vice versa, and the UK are not in the single market or the customs union. Since the center-left Labour party replaced the Conservatives in government in 2024, talk of a return to the customs union and alignment on other selected EU policy areas has been more frequent. But any return to full member status seems unlikely for now.
A decade after Brexit, youth in Britain want the EU back
Stabilization and association process – Western Balkan countries

The EU has not admitted a new member state since Croatia in 2013. Several nearby countries in the region are hoping to join the bloc, but must first fulfill a number of criteria under the EU's "stabilization and association process" designed for the "Western Balkans." These are: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia.

Under the plan, the EU has promised to "prepare Western Balkan partners for accession through economic reforms and investment and to bring some of the benefits of EU membership to citizens in the region."

States must first become official candidates for member state status by applying to the EU, with each of the member nations agreeing to them as a candidate country. Then follows a process of negotiation, such as that currently underway with Ukraine, Serbia and Montenegro. Finally, an accession treaty is prepared, which the European Commission, the European Council and the European Parliament must agree with. Only once that treaty has been signed and ratified by all member states and the candidate country will said country become an EU member.
EU enlargement: Who's slowing? Who's advancing? Who's next?

articles.title: Parents of NHL prospect hospitalized after collapse at team workout say he's a 'fighter'
articles.summary: The parents of Ontario prospect Matthew Mayich, who was drafted by the St. Louis Blues, are hoping for a miracle. The young hockey player is in hospital in critical condition.

image.caption: Christina and John Mayich are the parents of Matthew Mayich, a young hockey player who is currently in critical condition after a team workout. They spoke to CBC News from Phoenix, Ariz. (Andrew Hernandez/CBC)

blocks.text: The parents of an Ontario NHL prospect who is in critical condition after collapsing during a team workout say their son is "a fighter" and that they are not giving up on him.
Twenty-one-year-old Matthew Mayich, of Hamilton, was at an early-morning outdoor workout with the Arizona State University (ASU) hockey team on Aug. 20 when he collapsed.
"We know Matthew's a fighter and we're hoping he pulls through this," said Matthew's father, John. He and Matthew's mother, Christina, spoke to CBC News from Phoenix, Ariz.
Before the workout, Matthew was "perfectly healthy," according to Christina.
Now, their lawyer says, he’s "clinging to his life in a hospital bed."
The incident has made waves in the sports world, prompting the Professional Hockey Players’ Association to speak up about the lack of protections for young athletes.

"When athletes feel pressure to remain silent about an injury, illness, exhaustion or concern because they fear the consequences of speaking up, the system has failed them," said PHPA executive director Brian Ramsay in a statement on Sept. 10, which does not directly name Mayich.
"Athletes should never have to choose between their health and their careers. Period."
Family demands answers after hockey player collapses from 'military style' workout
He loved hockey but ‘he was a lot more than hockey’
Mayich started playing hockey around age five, according to John, and excelled.

He played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020, and then with the Ottawa 67's. In 2023, he was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues. His parents say they were his biggest fans, along with his younger brother and older sister, travelling everywhere to support him.
"He didn't care if he was at a small rink in Hamilton or a big rink in St. Louis with a lot of people — he just loves the game," John said.
"And he wasn't just about hockey. He was a lot more than just hockey."
Mayich’s parents describe him as "a little fireball," someone who people gravitate toward.
"Ever since he was young … he just lights up the room," said John.
Hockey player got heatstroke, lawyer says
When Mayich joined the ASU hockey team, it was the next rung on the ladder while chasing his NHL team.
The recent transfer to ASU was just getting settled into a new apartment, with his family looking forward to watching him play at the university.
His parents say they spoke with him briefly before the last workout, adding that he was excited and "ready to work."
Christina said one of Mayich’s teammates called her to tell her what happened, and that the family rushed to Phoenix to be by his side. They haven’t left.
"We were devastated," she said. "Heartbroken. Shocked. [It’s] just so hard to believe."
Mayich suffered heatstroke during the workout, according to the family’s Phoenix-based lawyer, Leonard Aragon, who is less optimistic than the parents that the young athlete will survive.
"I'm a lawyer, not a doctor, but I don't believe so," he told CBC News.
Workout designed to 'break the kids,' lawyer alleges
There were roughly 25 other players at the workout, according to John Mayich.

The morning session, which took place in advance of October's season opener, involved push-ups, running and drills where medicine balls were carried from one side of the field to the other, said Aragon.
The lawyer describes the session as "military-style," taking place in "overwhelming" heat and that water was withheld from players.
"[It] was designed to basically break the kids and try to put some sort of toughness or something like that into the kids at the beginning of the year," Aragon said.
He also says safety guidelines at the university were not followed.

"Protocols that ASU itself says should have been followed, such as monitoring people to see if they have heat problems or having a cool-down tub if someone has heatstroke or heat exhaustion — things like that didn't take place," he said. "And it led to this tragedy."
The university declined an interview request, citing an ongoing review.

It did not respond to questions about whether the individual who ran the workout was vetted and contracted by the university and whether there have been any consequences for the leadership team since the incident.

Instead, an ASU spokesperson referred CBC News to a statement issued on Sept. 3, stating the athletics program has "heat-illness guidelines in place" and that the morning workout included a "third party who had previously worked" with the team.
The statement said university police are investigating, "as they would anytime they are called to a serious incident."
Aragon calls the university’s failure to immediately call for an independent third-party investigation "a slap in the face to the family."
John Mayich's thoughts are also with the young athletes who witnessed what happened to his son.
"It was tragic what happened," he said. "I feel for them also. It's not easy to see that."
Is enough being done to protect athletes?
Athletes are highly competitive, seeking limited spots on sports teams, which is why protections for athletes are critical, says Adam Huxley, a hockey development coach based in Wainwright, Alta.

"When there's 30 players and 20 spots, I can see where the mindset of, 'Well, if I'm not feeling great or something's not going right, I don't want to be the one that says something, because then I seem like I'm the weak link,'" Huxley told CBC News.

He says there should be better education for players so they know when they are being pushed beyond their limits. Huxley also says it should be balanced with teams being able to tell their players it's OK to speak up.

"If you're in trouble, say something. If you feel like something's not going right or whatever — and that goes for the player that is involved in it, that goes [for] the teammates that are around [them], OK? And that goes for the staff," Huxley said. "Everyone's gonna learn from this."
In the statement issued by the PHPA, Ramsay said there is an obligation to keep pushing for a culture where speaking up about health and wellness is a strength not a weakness.
"That young man, on the cusp of his career in professional hockey, was failed by the system, the system that should have protected him," Ramsay said in the statement.
The National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA), which oversees student athletes in the United States, said a stated goal is to "ensure well-being … for college athletes."
An NCAA spokesperson declined to comment on the incident.
The NHL also did not respond to inquiries from CBC News.
Family waiting for a miracle
For now, Mayich's parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts and uncles are taking shifts at his bedside.

"Most of the kids usually come around him and they'll sing to him. There's Scripture-reading and prayers constantly. And we tell him funny stories, 'cause he was a funny guy, he was a jokester," Christina Mayich said.
"There's definitely a positive vibe in his room. There's something there that we just cannot explain. So much love, so much peace."
She says the family is taking it one day at a time.
"We're just continuing and asking the Lord to give us our miracle."

articles.title: Senators condemn Banga National High School shooting
articles.summary: Several senators condemned Friday"s shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato that left at least three students dead.

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 10:14pm
Several senators condemned Friday’s shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato that left at least three students dead.

The incident was the latest in a series of school shootings in the country this year. In June, three students were killed in a shooting at a high school in Tacloban City. Last month, a student opened fire on his schoolmates at Ateneo de Zamboanga, killing another student before turning the gun on himself.

“This cannot be our new normal. We need to pay attention to all the aspects that could lead to child endangerment—mental health, parental supervision, gun access, school security, nihilistic violent extremism (NVE), and the role of online platforms in fueling radicalization and violence among the youth,” Senator Risa Hontiveros said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Hontiveros chairs the Senate Committee on Women, Children, Family Relations and Gender Equality. She had also led investigations into the previous school shootings in Tacloban City and Zamboanga City.
NVE has been cited as a possible factor in some cases of school-based violence. It reportedly involves online communities that groom young people to commit violent acts with disregard for human life.
Senator Bam Aquino, who chairs the Senate education committee, also lamented the killings.

“Huwag tayong masanay na nangyayari ito. Huwag natin payagang maging normal ang school shooting sa ating bansa. Kailangan natin magsama-sama para sa kaligtasan at kinabukasan ng ating kabataan,” Aquino said in a separate statement.
(Let us not get used to this. We cannot allow school shootings to become normal. We need to band together for the safety and future of our children.)
Senator Loren Legarda, meanwhile, called for a deeper investigation into school shootings.

“We cannot keep responding to each tragedy by announcing the same measures anew. We have to determine what was promised after the previous incidents, what was actually done, and why those safeguards were still insufficient,” she said. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces launch inquest into sudden military collapse
articles.summary:
Rout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon position

A bitter inquest is under way among…

blocks.text: A bitter inquest is under way among Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces as to how what was being billed as a decisive assault on Sana’a, the Houthi-controlled capital, suddenly collapsed into a military rout.

More than 15 brigades were defeated as the country’s entire west coast fell into Houthi hands. Efforts are now being made to reorganise the anti-Houthi forces representing the UN-recognised Yemeni government in order to capture the Kahbob mountains, a strategic point from which to restrict Houthi forces moving closer to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.

Some Yemeni politicians are claiming that billions of dollars were offered to persuade the forces defending the west coast to abandon their position. It is thought as many as 30,000 well-equipped fighters retreated, raising questions about coordination, readiness and morale.

The claim made by the governor of Hadramaut, one of Yemen’s largest governorates, did not identify the source of the payment, but others have tried to draw conclusions from the past links between the United Arab Emirates and the pro-government National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh. The UAE left Yemen in January, but remains bitter at the role played by Saudi Arabia in forcing it out and in the outlawing of the separatist Southern Transitional Council.

The Yemeni Nobel peace prize winner Tawakkol Karman has called for an investigation, while another political activist, the Mocha resident Abdu Mukabib, described the withdrawal of forces from the now Houthi-held port city in the early hours of 10 September as a great betrayal.
Saleh’s National Resistance Forces have said they made a necessary tactical retreat.

Hours before, the Houthis had captured the headquarters of the National Resistance Forces operating along Yemen’s western coast, situated on the high ground of Jabal al-Nar (Fire Mountain) and supposed to contain six military brigades and sophisticated weaponry provided by Saudi Arabia.

Mukabib said on his Facebook page that by the time the Houthis entered the city at 6am their forces numbered less than 20: two military vehicles, each carrying five people, and four motorcycles, each carrying two people.

He said that what happened, in his words, caused “humiliation” and betrayal to those who trusted the forces they fought alongside. “We are not accusing anyone, but they all participated in betraying us, conspiring against us, selling out our cause and abandoning us.
“It was not a withdrawal from weakness or lack of equipment and supplies, but rather a cowardly and shameful withdrawal.”

The National Resistance Forces said they had withdrawn after the death of 500 of their soldiers and to prevent encirclement. Saleh has said he is now forming the “Tihami Resistance”, a group that was entirely independent of Yemen national forces.

Others point to explanations for the reverse including poor command and control communications that led to slow decision-making, high-level Houthi intelligence and divisions within the anti-Houthi military forces, including the influence of Saudi commanders.

Alongside the inadequacies of the UN-backed forces, the Houthis have become an increasingly sophisticated army, bolstered by Iranian intelligence. They have benefited from the cut-price nature of modern warfare, using cheap drones to harass maritime traffic. But more than 10 years in control of many of Yemen’s key regions and the occasional payoff from Saudi Arabia have swelled their coffers enough to not only buy ballistic missiles, but develop their own indigenous weapon-making infrastructure, becoming less reliant on Iran in the process.
Iranian officials insist the Houthis are not a simple proxy force, but have their own unified command structure and set of priorities.

The inquest into what is widely regarded as a military catastrophe is not entirely retrospective. Both Yemen government and Saudi forces are urgently reviewing the lessons of defeat to better understand whether the Houthi gains can still be reversed.

It was claimed that a limited force from the Giants Brigades, a group once linked with the UAE-backed southern separatists, managed to repel the Houthi advance and recapture positions in the days before the fall of Mocha, which could have served as a springboard for regaining the initiative. However, the withdrawal of neighbouring National Resistance units weakened this advance and turned it into a series of retreats.

Prof Dr Abdulwahab al-Awaj at Taiz University in Yemen said: “The collapse of the western coastal fronts is not merely a conventional military defeat, but a warning sign of a breakdown in coordination and trust among the anti-Houthi forces. The Houthis exploited this breakdown more than any decisive military superiority.

“Regaining the initiative cannot be achieved simply by sending reinforcements. What is needed is a reorganisation of government forces and allied formations under a unified operational vision, addressing security gaps, and building genuine trust on the ground to prevent a recurrence of this scenario.”

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz attacks spill oil into Persian Gulf
articles.summary: As war disrupts one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, satellite images reveal that oil is spreading toward protected coral reefs and mangrove forests.

image.caption: Oil coats the coast of Qeshm Island, Iran, on August 13, 2026, after a spill reached the shore from the Strait of HormuzImage: Sanaz/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: A dark, muddied patch of blue, incongruent with the rest of the ocean; a winding thread of silvery white; a reflective metallic sheen — these are some of the telltale signs on a satellite image that oil may be leaking into the water.

Experts have identified these and many other visual signaturesin the Strait of Hormuz, leading them to conclude that there's an environmental crisis playing out amid the US-Iran war, as tankers are struck by missiles, set on fire or sunk.
One recent example: In June, a Russian tanker carrying about 800,000 barrels of oil stranded off the coast of Oman, causing a major spill.

Earlier in the war, there were as many as 85 large oil-laden tankers stuck in the Strait — that number has since dropped to 13, according to Greenpeace. Each stranded tanker, plus every other vessel trying to move through the waterway, poses a distinct risk for attack and thus a spill. Since the start of the war, the environmental organization has used satellite imagery to track more than 100 spills.

There are likely several other spills that we don't know of, amid widespread GPS spoofing in the region that causes ships to broadcast false positions. Greenpeace released a report this week calling the situation an "ecological catastrophe" and pinpointing a number of oil slicks that are extending into protected and fragile ecosystems.

"People should be concerned," Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief, told DW. The war has taken "a very, very heavy toll on the environment," she said, with the damage now reaching new scales.
Where is the oil spreading?

Greenpeace identified five major oil slicks earlier this week with a total visible area of 240 square kilometers (about 90 square miles) in the Strait of Hormuz. That's about four times the size of Manhattan.

These patches of oil floating on the ocean's surface are getting smaller — now about 80 square kilometers — according to more up-to-date satellite images, as weather conditions have likely made the slicks disperse. But that does not mean the ecological impact is any less severe, Noelle said. "Oil can also sink into the sediment and impact the ecosystems for years and years."

What's concerning is where the slicks were identified. One was found near Musandam National Park, a protected area in Oman that's home to coral reefs, sea life and important breeding grounds for sea birds. Another is close to Iran's Minab River Delta and its protected mudflats and mangrove forests. This kind of damage can take decades for ecosystems to recover from.
Tracking an unclear picture
It's hard to say exactly how far the oil has reached and how severe the damage is.
"What we have put out is the conservative estimate," Noelle said. "It might be worse. It's definitely not better."

Greenpeace and other environmental organizations are relying on satellite images provided by the Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites. They're part of the European Union's Earth observation program and are publicly available.

There are also private satellite providers such as Planet Labs that tend to have higher-resolution images. But they've limited access to satellite imagery during the war to prevent their data from being used for military targeting. And there are limits to on-the-ground reports too.

"We don't have a lot of information coming from the country itself, both in Iran as well as the Gulf states," Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher who uses open-source methods at the Dutch peace organization Pax, told DW. "There is quite restrictive policies of people posting imagery from what's happening on the shore."
The toll on wildlife and people
Oil pooling into the Gulf poses a number of threats — both to biodiversity and to humans.

Oil can be deadly for seabirds. It coats their feathers, reducing their natural waterproofing and buoyancy, making it harder to stay afloat, fly, and hunt for food. Even small amounts of oil can damage eggs too, causing them not to hatch or to be born with deformities.
Mangrove habitats, which provide safe harbor for coastal species, are also hit hard.

"Mangroves have aerial roots, and the oil is covering these roots like a film and actually hindering the mangroves in exchanging gases," Noelle said. "They're kind of suffocated by the oil. Most of the time, it leads to the trees dying."

The risks extend to people, as well. Coastal communities rely on fish that die off after being exposed to oil. And oil spills contaminate water used for Gulf states' drinking supply. Desalination — or converting seawater into drinkable water — is where 90% of drinking water in Kuwait comes from, along with about 86% in Oman and 70% in Saudi Arabia.

blocks.caption: Vessels anchor near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, OmanImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Cleanup is no easy fix.

"It's unlikely that it will be addressed quickly, because of the war," Zwijnenburg said. "War in general makes it very difficult to respond fast to these kind of emergencies. There are a range of limitations because of the military movement, because of mines — so it's very difficult to get vessels and cleanup operations to start."
Environmental groups have pointed to the war in Iran — and the rising scale of oil spills it has caused — as further evidence that the world needs to move away from its dependence on fossil fuels.

"The most sustainable long-term damage prevention for things like that would be to reduce and ultimately end our dependency on oil and gas," Noelle said. "Because, as long as our energy systems and transport routes are centered around fossil fuels, there will be a continued environmental risk."
How much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz?

articles.title: Dual citizenship means Germany now in competition for talent
articles.summary: Coach Jürgen Klopp has named several players to his first Germany squad who are eligible to play for other countries. Some still aren't committed to Germany long term.

image.caption: Younes Ebnoutalib opened the season for Frankfurt with a hat trick in BerlinImage: Inaki Esnaola/Gonzales Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: When Jürgen Klopp named his oversized squad for Germany for the upcoming international break, a number of other national team coaches will have taken notice.
Among them was Mohamed Ouahbi of Morocco, who lamented that he had already had Eintracht Frankfurt striker Younes on his radar since last season.
"He had a profile that interested us. I spoke to him on the phone and explained the Morocco project to him—without making any promises," Ouahbi said.
If the 23-year-old Ebnoutalib sees any action in the UEFA Nations League over the next couple of weeks, as expected, he will be cap-tied to Germany – and ineligible to play for Morocco in the future.
Several players with multiple options

This is by no means a unique situation, as a growing number of Germany players in recent years hold other citizenships through their parents and thus have other options for their international careers.

This applies to several other members of Klopp's 44-man squad. Vitaly Janelt, whose father moved to Germany to play professional ice hockey, is also eligible to represent Czechia. Bambasé Conté's father is from Guinea, and Josha Vagnoman has an Ivorian father. Finn Dahmen has an English mother, while fellow goalkeeper Noah Atubolu has Nigerian roots. Said El Mala's father hails from Lebanon, and Brajan Gruda's father was an Albania international.

blocks.caption: Said El Mala and Brajan Gruda have represented Germany at the under-21 levelImage: Marco Steinbrenner/DeFodi Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: All of them were all born and raised in Germany and have represented the country a tyouth levels. Vagnoman has even made two senior international appearances for Germany, though he has yet to play a competitive match.
High number of dual nationals

There are also numerous established Germany players who could have chosen another nation. These include Felix Nmecha (England), Kevin Schade (Nigeria), Jamal Musiala (Nigeria, England), Karim Adeyemi (Nigeria, Romania), Jonathan Tah and Serge Gnabry (Ivory Coast), Malick Thiaw (Senegal, Finland), Nathaniel Brown (USA), Nadiem Amiri (Afghanistan), Aleksandar Pavlovic (Serbia), Waldemar Anton (Russia), Yann Aurel Bisseck (Cameroon), and Ridle Baku (DR Congo).
The men's national team reflects German society as a whole; according to the Federal Statistical Office, 21.8 million of Germany's approximately 83 million inhabitants have an immigrant background.

"More than 40% of children in Germany under the age of five have a migration background. This means they will later have the option to play for one country or the other," Andreas Rettig, the German FA's (DFB) outgoing managing director for sport told DW prior to last summer's World Cup.
This forces the DFB to compete with other countries for talent for its national teams, and it hasn't always been successful.
A prime example is Ibrahim Maza of Bayer Leverkusen. Born and raised in Berlin to an Algerian father and a Vietnamese mother, he holds not just German but also Algerian and Vietnamese citizenship.

blocks.caption: Ibrahim Maza (second from right) chose to represent Algeria rather than GermanyImage: Thor Wegner/DeFodi Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: The midfielder possesses many qualities that could help Germany, yet two years ago he opted to play for Algeria and represented the "Desert Foxes" at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and the 2026 World Cup.

Germany also missed out on Paul Wanner and Can Uzun. Wanner, a top prospect developed at Bayern Munich, chose Austria—his mother's home country. Can Uzun of Eintracht Frankfurt has been playing for Turkey since September 2024. Both took part in last summer's World Cup.
International break a cap-tying opportunity
Had Maza, Wanner, and Uzun chosen Germany instead, each of them would have stood a good chance of being named to Klopp's first squad as national team coach.

With this international break featuring four instead of the previous customary two matches – and to see as many players as possible, Klopp named two squads for this break – meaning every player selected has a strong chance of getting playing time.

The upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures—away against the Netherlands, home and away against Greece, and at home against Serbia, are all competitive matches. This means that even if it wasn't the primary factor in his selection process, over the next couple of weeks, Klopp could wind up cap-tying a few more players for Germany.

articles.title: PH condemns China Coast Guard aggression in West Philippine Sea collision
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said there was “no justification” for the China Coast Guard"s (CCG) aggressive actions that resulted in a minor collision with a Philippine civilian vessel in…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 9:46pm

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said there was “no justification” for the China Coast Guard’s (CCG) aggressive actions that resulted in a minor collision with a Philippine civilian vessel in the West Philippine Sea on Friday.
The incident involved China Coast Guard vessel CCG-21585 and the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat (MMOV-3015), the DFA said.

"The Department of Foreign Affairs condemns the actions of China Coast Guard vessel. ...There is no justification for the CCG vessel to undertake aggressive actions against a Philippine civilian law enforcement vessel, and cause damage to the ship and endanger the safety of the civilian crew," the department said in a statement.
It stressed the BFAR vessel was merely conducting routine and lawful humanitarian activities to support Filipino fisherfolk in the West Philippine Sea.

The DFA said the CCG vessel's "illegal, coercive, aggressive and dangerous acts" are inconsistent with China's obligations under international law. This includes the UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award, the 1972 International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS), and the 1974 Safety of Life at Sea Convention.

"The Philippines calls on China to respect Philippine sovereign rights within its exclusive economic zone in accordance with UNCLOS as affirmed by the 2016 Arbitral Award, exercise restraint and avoid actions that could further escalate tensions in the region," the DFA said.

Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for WPS Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said the CCG vessel rammed the BRP Datu Magat Salamat while the Philippine vessel was carrying out its maritime patrol and fuel subsidy mission.
Tarriela said that at 11:04 a.m., the Chinese vessel reportedly cut across the stern of the BFAR vessel at a distance of only about 10 meters.
At 11:13 a.m., while the BRP Datu Magat Salamat was maintaining its course, the Chinese vessel repeated the maneuver and made contact with the BFAR vessel, striking it.
The Philippine vessel sustained damage on its starboard side, including bent, broken, and detached metal stanchions and support structures. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software error
articles.summary: UK ministers say report into incident leaves questions unanswered over why problem was not discovered and fixed earlier

blocks.text: A software defect in part of the UK’s air traffic control system corrupted flight data “in the space of a millisecond”, leading to a six-hour outage and mass airline cancellations and delays across the UK last week, National Air Traffic Services has said.
But ministers said that the report into the incident still left questions unanswered, saying they needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said the industry regulator the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) would now “check their findings” and investigate Nats’ plans.

Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted after the Nats failure on Tuesday 8 September, which initially only stopped flights departing in the London area but eventually spread to disrupt travel across the UK and beyond by the evening.
Airlines called for the dismissal of the Nats chief executive officer, Martin Rolfe, after the third major air traffic control failure in the UK since summer 2023.
However, Rolfe said the incident was unrelated to the previous failures and dismissed speculation that it was caused by military intervention.
The preliminary report said that the failure was a software defect in part of the National Airspace System, which allocates codes to individual aircraft to identify flights on radar.

The report said that while a manual request for an aircraft code was being processed, another request paused it, adding: “When processing of the aircraft code request resumed, the software defect meant it did not resume correctly and the resulting output was corrupted, and affected some subsequent flight data updates. This happened in the space of a millisecond.”
Rolfe said: “The issue has been identified and mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety tested and deployed.”

Nats said restrictions were put in place across the UK so that the system could be restarted. The restrictions were in place for six hours and it took more than two days for the backlog of passenger disruption to be cleared, with hundreds of thousands of passengers’ travel plans disrupted.

Rolfe added: “I would like to apologise again, very sincerely, to everyone who was affected last week. It’s our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong. However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question.”
However, Alexander said: “The disruption we saw last week was completely unacceptable and I know how frustrating it was for passengers, airlines and airports.”
after newsletter promotion

She said she had received Nats’ report, adding: “While I am pleased to see that the safety of passengers was protected, it’s clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos.

“I have therefore tasked the CAA with conducting an independent review to check Nats’ findings and investigate their investment plans to enhance resilience in the future, along with regulatory accountability.

“It is crucial that our national infrastructure is fit for the future, and this government will make sure the aviation sector is as resilient as possible, so passengers can get to where they need to be.”
The CAA’s review will be published within six months.

articles.title: British Sikh man granted bail in India nine years after arrest
articles.summary:
Jagtar Singh Johal, from Scotland, was arrested after wedding in Punjab on alleged terrorism offences

Jagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested in India in 2017 in connection…

blocks.text: Jagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested in India in 2017 in connection with alleged terrorism offences, has been granted bail by a Delhi court.
Johal, from Scotland, was arrested for his alleged role in funding the Khalistan Liberation Force, which had carried out targeted killings in India’s Punjab region.

His full trial has been repeatedly deferred by the authorities in the federal court but largely similar conspiracy charges were dismissed by a court in Punjab last year. Throughout his detention the prosecution has failed to produce verifiable evidence, leading to the deferred hearings.

Johal, now 39, travelled to India to marry his fiancee in late 2017. On 4 November, three weeks after the wedding, the couple were shopping with a relative in the Punjab city of Jalandhar when a group of men took Johal from his car, placed a black hood over his head and put him in an unmarked vehicle. He claims he was then denied access to a lawyer and tortured in an attempt to extract a confession. A question remains over whether he was arrested following a tip-off from British intelligence services.

Commenting on Friday’s ruling, Johal’s Scotland-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “The past two years has been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at the supreme court and back to the high court. I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment.”
He added of previous hearings: “Whenever the evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.

“How long will this sick joke of a legal process be allowed to continue? We’re obviously delighted that Jagtar will soon be released, but he won’t be truly free until he is back in Dumbarton, with his wife and family.”

blocks.caption: Gurpreet Singh Johal has fought tirelessly for his brother’s release. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: Gurpreet Johal, who also lives in Dumbarton, has lobbied a succession of UK foreign secretaries, who have repeatedly admitted the case has dragged on too long, but have been reluctant to call publicly for his release on the grounds that they should not interfere in the judiciary of another country.
after newsletter promotion
The UK government recently appointed Alistair Burt as a special envoy for complex consular cases and he has met Gurpreet Johal in Scotland to discuss the case.

Dan Dolan, the deputy executive director of Reprieve, one of the organisation’s fighting for Johal’s release, said: “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way. The conditions attached are likely to be onerous. We must also remember that Jagtar will still be facing the death penalty in eight cases against him, despite these cases essentially duplicating trumped-up charges on which he has already been fully acquitted.”
Chris Esdaile, a senior legal adviser to Redress, another organisaiton representing Johal, said granting bail “can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention”.
He added: “The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent.”

Johal’s lawyers said they were still awaiting the details of what would happen next in relation to posting bail terms. While the judges’ order was that Jagtar should be released on bail, he remained in custody while judges confirmed his bail conditions, which may be stringent. The court must also confirm the sums of money that must be posted as a bond.
