articles.title: Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron
articles.summary: The French president says he has tasked the government with protecting critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

blocks.text: French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France has intensified.

In a news conference at the Elysee Palace, Macron said he had called on the French government to prepare a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites in the face of this threat.
He said France had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks which would not be left "without a response".
A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.
The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said.

"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
Macron added that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks.
He also announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission.

"In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said.
"It will also be an opportunity to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves."

articles.title: Beethoven and Andy Warhol: Rebel icons on show in Bonn
articles.summary: The new exhibition "Beethoven by Warhol" at the Beethoven House in Bonn presents the pop artist's late masterpiece: a picture of Ludwig van Beethoven. The exhibition shares the story of the work with…

image.caption: The Mona Lisa of the Beethoven House: Andy Warhol's take on the composerImage: Meike Böschemeyer/Beethovenhaus

blocks.text: Andy Warhol portrait of Ludwig van Beethoven offers an unprecedented visual take on the great composer.

Warhol's 1987 silkscreen dispenses with the stern face usually seen on historical portraits and statues of the musical genius. Instead, Warhol uses pop art's vivid colors and striking visual language to turn Beethoven into a modern icon.

Originally conceived as a commercial work for the pop art guru's New York City studio, known as The Factory, the image was produced in a limited edition of 60 and proved to be one of the most innovative artistic engagements with Ludwig van Beethoven in the 20th century.
Warhol created the famous Beethoven color silkscreen prints just a few weeks before his sudden death on February 22, 1987. The series is among his final works.

blocks.caption: The final silkscreen print was preceded by numerous attempts in many colorsImage: Beethoven-Haus Bonn

blocks.text: How did Warhol approach Beethoven as a subject? And in what context did the work emerge in its numerous colored variations? A special exhibition, "Beethoven by Warhol," on show until April 2027 at the Beethoven House in Bonn — the composer's birthplace — explores these questions and more.
Like-minded geniuses?

The exhibition presents rare works that visitors would otherwise never get to see. Over the course of three years, the team of curators at the Beethoven House and Archive Bonn, led by Malte Boecker, unearthed these valuable pieces from the depths of archives and private collections.

blocks.caption: In 1986, Andy Warhol had his picture taken with a bust of BeethovenImage: 2026 The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc./Licensed by Artists Rights Society (ARS)

blocks.text: Alongside Warhol's iconic depiction of Beethoven, visitors can see drawings the artist did while searching for his Beethoven motif in Bonn. There are also proofs of prints that document his exploration of the series' color scheme.
The curators highlight an elaborately crafted Beethoven print on canvas, which belongs to an anonymous collector from the Rhineland.
Curator Silke Bettermann said that, with such works, "Warhol tells us: Look here! This man, Beethoven, is completely modern! He's a superstar!"
Warhol's approach to subjects
Whenever something looks effortless and easy, there's almost always a great deal of work behind it. The same is true of Warhol's Beethoven series.

In his research process, Warhol compared numerous depictions of the composer before developing his own concept. He also did drawings based on likenesses of Beethoven, including the statue of the composer at Münsterplatz in Bonn.

blocks.caption: Boecker is director of the Beethovenhaus and the initiator of the projectImage: Thomas Banneyer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ultimately, Warhol decided to base his work on the iconic portrait by Joseph Karl Stieler, painted in 1820 on commission from the Frankfurt couple Franz and Antonie Brentano — a merchant family and patrons of the arts who were friends with the composer. The portrait sought to capture not only Beethoven's outward appearance but also his rebellious personality.

Warhol adopts the graphic design of Stieler's work, transforming its colors and overlaying it with a handwritten Beethoven score. However, rather than using the notes of the "Credo" of the "Missa Solemnis," as Stieler did, he chose music from the "Moonlight Sonata," probably Beethoven's most famous work. "Warhol's Beethoven speaks to us quite literally through and by means of his music," curator Silke Bettermann told DW.
Sports star at Beethoven House

Bonn-based Warhol gallerist Hermann Wünsche played a key role in the creation of Warhol's Beethoven works. He not only visited the artist in New York, but also brought him to the Rhineland several times. It's thanks to Wünsche that the artist created numerous Germany-related pieces, including the portraits of Chancellor Willy Brandt from 1976 and soccer star Toni Schumacher, whom Warhol portrayed in 1983.

blocks.caption: Warhol depicted Toni Schumacher in a print. The German soccer star also came to the exhibition's openingImage: Meike Böschemeyer/Beethovenhaus

blocks.text: The exhibition's organizers brought the work depicting Schumacher to Bonn — on loan from the soccer star's private collection. The former goalkeeper himself also paid a visit.
In 1983, Schumacher sat as a model for Warhol. "It really gave me goosebumps!" he said.

Schumacher recalls his meeting with the US artist: "Back then, in the mid-1980s, in all modesty, I was already a star, too. But then Andy Warhol came along. And when we were together in the same room, I felt like I was looking at a superstar, so I took a bit of a back seat."
Warhol and music
Also on display for the first time at the Beethoven House is a unique collection of record covers designed by Warhol, assembled by Belgian collector and Warhol expert Guy Minnebach.

blocks.caption: Also displayed is a private collection from Belgium showcasing Warhol's album coversImage: Meike Böschemeyer/Beethovenhaus

blocks.text: Over the course of three decades, Andy Warhol designed strikingly beautiful and individual covers for more than 50 records.

The range extends from a relatively classical, yet already whimsically playful, Mendelssohn record featuring Vladimir Horowitz, whom Warhol also knew personally, to the legendary jeans cover with a real zipper for The Rolling Stones' "Sticky Fingers" (1971) and the famous banana album cover for The Velvet Underground & Nico (1967).
According to eyewitness accounts, music played continuously at Warhol's studio. His record covers offer a glimpse into the artist's musical tastes. Beethoven, notably, is not among them.
Wolfram Weimer: 'We need more Beethoven'

The Warhol exhibition is the prelude to an important event at the Beethoven House. In March 2027, people around the world will commemorate the 200th anniversary of Beethoven's death with a special edition of the Beethoven Festival.

blocks.caption: Germany's state minister for culture and media, Wolfram Weimer, attended the opening in BonnImage: Meike Böschemeyer/Beethovenhaus

blocks.text: "This exhibition is a wonderful opening to the Beethoven commemorative year," Wolfram Weimer, Germany's state minister for culture and media, told DW. As patron of the exhibition at the Beethoven House, he traveled to Bonn to see it and speak at the opening ceremony. "Today, we need more Beethoven," he said during his speech.

"Beethoven was not only a musical genius who delighted the world with the greatest musical works of art imaginable," Weimer said. The composer also embodied the idea of freedom: "He was a rebel, he broke norms, and he questioned the power structures of his time. He was a messenger of freedom, and that is a good message for us today. We need more freedom today, too!"
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Pakistan suicide bombing targets police facility in Kohat
articles.summary: A police official said the explosion killed at least 16 people, injuring many more. The attacker targeted a police facility and damaged a mosque at the site. The president blamed the attack on the…

image.caption: Emergency services rushed to the scene of the attack, which targeted a police headquarters in KohatImage: Basit Shah/AFP

blocks.text: A bomb attack in Kohat, Pakistan, near the Afghan border killed at least 16 people, police said on Friday.
No group immediately claimed responsibility but Pakistan's president blamed the Tehreek-e-Taliban (TTP).
Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan's Taliban rulers are fraught, with Islamabad alleging that the TTP uses safe havens across the Afghan border to plot and train for attacks in Pakistan.

blocks.caption: Security personnel tried to guard the site following Friday's attackImage: Basit Shah/AFP

blocks.text: What do we know about the attack?
Stated casualty figures varied amid ongoing rescue operations on Friday after the explosives-laden car caused a large explosion and damaged a mosque at a police compound.

But provincial police chief Zulfikar Hameed told Reuters that at least 16 people, including five police personnel, were killed in the attack. A rescue official also told AFP that five police officers, 10 civilians and the attacker had died.
Figures on the number of wounded also varied but were put above 30 or even 50.
Police said in a statement that the blast occurred near a mosque as officers, their relatives and other civilians were worshipping inside.
They referred to it as a suicide attack.
Police also said that its forces and other attackers engaged in a subsequent gun battle after at least two other militants tried to to enter the facility.

blocks.caption: Kohat, a city of around 220,000 people south of Peshawar, is fairly close to the Afghan borderImage: B.S. Gillani/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Government blames TTP amid attack in Afghan border area
No group claimed responsibility for the attack in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack and expressed sorrow over the casualties. He directed authorities to accelerate rescue operations. The Interior Ministry said that the "cowardly actions" of the attackers would not weaken "the nation's resolve."
President Asif Ali Zardari appeared to assign the blame to the TTP Tehreek-e-Taliban group.
"The complete elimination of Fitna-al-Khawarij and terrorists operating with foreign backing it essential for national security," Zardari said, using another term for the TTP.
Pakistan blames the increase of attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the border province of Balochistan further south in large part on the Taliban administration in neighboring Afghanistan.
How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan
The Taliban rejects these allegations.
The accusations have sparked a bitter rift and even incidents of armed conflict between the neighboring countries.
Pakistan has carried out airstrikes it says targets militants taking refuge on Afghan soil, including this June.
Authorities in Kabul have in turn decried these attacks and reported civilian casualties.

articles.title: Germany: Is it possible to replace the chancellor?
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's record-low approval ratings have emboldened his opponents. There are three ways to remove a chancellor from office in Germany.

image.caption: Sixteen months into office, Friedrich Merz has record low approval ratings, triggering a debate abour his futureImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: It is the hot topic this week in Berlin: Does German Chancellor Friedrich Merz still have the backing of his own party, the Christian Democrats (CDU), and the coalition partners, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)? Will he be ousted? How would that work? Can he just step down?

Support for the chancellor has reached a record low: In the latest Deutschlandtrend representative survey, conducted by pollsters Infratest-Dimap for German public broadcaster ARD in early September, only 13% of respondents said Merz was doing a good job.
In early September, Merz's CDU suffered a resounding loss in the state of Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentary election, seeing the party's result halved from the 2021 election.
The election result has reinforced criticism of Merz, even from within his own ranks, and his communication style, which frequently alienates his audience.
But Merz remains chancellor. What are the options to change that? Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, grants the position a strong standing. German chancellors are not so easy to unseat.

items: Option 1: Resignation

blocks.text: Merz himself can decide to resign for any reason. That would not necessarily mean the end of the coalition government he leads. An example: In May 1974, then Chancellor Willy Brandt of the SPD resigned after a spy from the communist East Germany (DDR) was discovered to have been working in his inner circle. The governing parties, the SPD and the business-oriented Free Democrats (FDP), quickly agreed to continue their alliance.

Only 10 days later, Finance Minister Helmut Schmidt, also of the SPD, was elected as the new chancellor. To do this, an absolute majority of all lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, was needed (not only those present during the vote). This majority is called the "chancellor majority". Schmidt achieved this effortlessly, eventually got reelected and remained head of the German government for 8 years.
How likely is Merz to step down? Today's chancellor seems determined not to give up.

items: Option 2: A constructive vote of no-confidence

blocks.text: If a new majority were formed through alliances in the Bundestag or if a chancellor fell so far out of favor that their own supporters no longer believed in them, the instrument of a "constructive vote of no-confidence" could come into play. That means the majority of lawmakers vote in favor of a new candidate for chancellor.

An example: Helmut Schmidt of the SPD, lost the support of his junior coalition partner, the FDP, in 1982. The FDP wanted to push through changes to economic policy, which Schmidt rejected. They joined forces with the conservatives from the CDU and CSU, and jointly put CDU leader Helmut Kohl forward as a new chancellor. He won a majority in parliament, replaced Schmidt and moved into the chancellor's office where he remained for 16 years.

The probability of this happening in Merz's case is very remote. The conservatives and Social Democrats do not want to end their coalition. There is no clear rival candidate for Merz. North Rhine-Westphalia's State Premier Hendrik Wüst of the CDU is seen as a possible successor, but has not made a step forward. Besides: The CDU is usually very loyal toward its political leaders; ousting the chancellor via a vote of no confidence on the open stage of the Bundestag is simply unthinkable for most conservative lawmakers.

items: Option 3: A confidence vote

blocks.text: Germany's parliament cannot simply dissolve itself and call new elections. Lawmakers can, however, call a confidence vote on the chancellor and his government. Several chancellors have already used this mechanism, coupling it with a vote on a contentious issue.

As chancellor in November 2001, Gerhard Schröder (SPD) put forward a confidence vote in the Bundestag and linked it with the question of whether his government should deploy the German military to Afghanistan to support the NATO mission led by the United States following the September 11 attacks. Schröder won, remained in office and continued with his military policy.
Merz has already said he sees no point in calling for a confidence vote. There are also no signs of large breakaway movements from members of his coalition in Parliament.

If a chancellor loses a confidence vote, the Bundestag can be dissolved and fresh elections called. Following the defeat in the Bundestag, the chancellor can ask the German President to dissolve parliament and call voters to the polls. The president is not obliged to do so, but usually does.
It seems that Merz has ruled out this option. Neither the SPD nor the conservative Union (of CDU/CSU) are interested in calling new elections at a time when their approval ratings are low.
So will the government remain the same? Right now, it seems so. However, things have been so dynamic in recent days and weeks in Berlin political circles that nothing should be ruled out.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Ronaldo named in first Portugal squad since World Cup - at age of 41
articles.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo is named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus for their upcoming Nations League games.

blocks.text: Cristiano Ronaldo has been named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, ending speculation the 41-year-old could retire from international football.
Ronaldo refused to confirm whether he would continue to play for his country after Portugal's World Cup round-of-16 defeat by eventual winners Spain in July.
But the Al-Nassr forward is part of a 25-man group chosen for Portugal's four Nations League games between 24 September and 4 October.
Jesus has replaced Roberto Martinez, who stepped down as Portugal coach after their World Cup exit.
The 72-year-old was Ronaldo's club boss last season, when the pair helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Pro League for the first time in seven years.
The former Manchester United Real Madrid forward, who announced that this summer's World Cup would be his last, was in tears after Portugal's World Cup exit.
When asked if he would keep playing for his country, he said: "I will meet the family and take decisions with a calm head."
This sparked speculation he could follow his great rival Lionel Messi and retire from international football.
Ronaldo will turn 42 before next summer's Nations League finals and will be 43 by Euro 2028.
The oldest player in the history of the Euros is Ronaldo's former Portugal team-mate Pepe, who was 41 and 130 days for his last game at Euro 2024.
Manchester United pair Diogo Dalot and Bruno Fernandes are also in the squad, along with Ruben Dias (Manchester City) and Pedro Neto (Chelsea).
Portugal are at home to Wales on 24 September (19:45 BST) and away to Norway three days later. They then play in Denmark on 1 October and return home to host Norway on 4 October.

articles.title: Banga High School Shooting: Grade 9 suspect warned classmates, 'Go home'
articles.summary: The suspect in the Banga National High School shooting incident, which killed three students in the South Cotabato town, was a Grade 9 student and the son of an employee of the Department of…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 8:25pm

The suspect in the Banga National High School shooting incident, which killed three students in the South Cotabato town, was a Grade 9 student and the son of an employee of the Department of Education in Region 12.
Banga Mayor Albert Palencia said the shooter reportedly told his friends after lunch that they should go home. He warned them that he might do something bad.

“May isang estudyante na nagsabi sa kaibigan niya na after lunch, ‘dapat mag-uwi na kayo, kasi meron akong gagawin after lunch. Baka madamay pa kayo’. Yung mga classmate niya, nagtawa, akala niya, linoloko lang sila ng shooter,” Palencia told Super Radyo dzBB.
(There was a student that told his friends that after lunch, ‘go home, because I will do something after lunch.’ The classmates laughed, thinking that the shooter was joking.)
It was said that the student left his classroom and opened fire in the adjacent classroom.
Palencia said the shooter brought two magazines for a 9 mm gun. After he opened fire on other students, the shooter reportedly turned the gun on himself after changing magazines.
The student reportedly got the gun from his own father.
“Yung papa niya, shooter din. At saka empleyado ng DepEd Region XII. Kaya 'yung baril, tinatago sa vault, sinira ng bata 'yung vault at saka dinala 'yung baril sa eskwelahan,” Palencia said.
(His father was a shooter, also. And an employee of DepEd Region XII. So the gun was hidden in the vault, the kid broke the vault, and then he brought the gun to school.)
The mayor said he learned that the mother of the shooter was planning to take her child to seek psychiatric help.
The shooter’s sibling was also a teacher in the high school.
His father was in General Santos, teaching about child safety. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: 'No compromises': Far-right AfD has few potential partners
articles.summary: Germany's far-right AfD party is riding high after its latest electoral triumph in Saxony-Anhalt. But one question remains: Does it actually want to govern?

image.caption: The AfD's election winners in Saxony-Anhalt celebrated their victory by singing the national anthemImage: Ronny Hartmann/AFP

blocks.text: With just under 44% of the vote, the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as by far the strongest party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. It fell only narrowly short of an absolute majority in the newly elected state parliament, and with it the opportunity to govern on its own.

From the outset, the AfD made clear that governing alone was its preferred outcome. Only by avoiding having to compromise with coalition partners, the party argued, could it fully implement its agenda, which included compulsory work schemes for asylum-seekers, citizen patrols monitoring migration-related issues, and the abolition of all public funding for democracy and civic engagement programs.
After AfD's record result: Voices from Saxony-Anhalt

While Germany was debating whether the so-called "firewall" against the AfD was an appropriate means of protecting democracy, the party itself had long since built a wall of its own. For years, it has dismissed its political rivals as "cartel parties," effectively grouping them together with criminal organizations.

Teresa Haussmann of the University of Potsdam has been studying the AfD and other populist parties for years. In her view, the AfD sees "all other parties as part of a political elite that must be opposed."
Ulrich Siegmund: 'No compromises!'
On election night, at the height of the celebrations, the AfD's emerging star and lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, adopted a notably more conciliatory tone than he had done throughout his campaign.
"As a democrat, I extend my hand to all political forces willing to pursue a fundamental change of course with us," he said in an interview with German public broadcaster ARD.
Moments later, however, he qualified the offer: "There will be no bending on my part, no compromises."

blocks.caption: Siegmund (center, giving the thumbs-up sign) and his AfD colleagues were all smiles the day after the Saxony-Anhalt voteImage: Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: Within the AfD, compromise is frequently portrayed as a sign of weakness or a betrayal of principle. According to Haussmann, this is typical of populist parties not only in Germany but in many other countries as well.

"The basic premise is that a clearly identifiable popular will exists. If that is the case, then there can be only one correct political course. Any compromise would call that premise into question, because it would mean acknowledging that more than one legitimate path exists," she said.

Little remains of the conciliatory tone struck on election night. As they did throughout the campaign, senior AfD politicians are once again targeting their political opponents with insults and inflammatory rhetoric.
Few power-sharing options for AfD

In fact, the parties most likely to be considered potential coalition partners are often the ones the AfD attacks most fiercely. At present, the most obvious candidates are the center-right conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and the smaller left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).
Merz, Weidel clash in parliament after AfD election win

Immediately after the election victory, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel launched a blistering attack on the chancellor's party, declaring: "The CDU/CSU will never be able to win another federal election. That's a fact."

The Christian Democrats were the big losers of the election in Saxony-Anhalt. Some conservatives believe the party has drifted too far to the left — and it's precisely those disillusioned voters that the AfD is hoping to attract.

At the same time, the AfD has adopted increasingly radical rhetoric and, in Saxony-Anhalt, is classified by the security authorities as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization. The primary reason is that the party questions the legal equality of Germans with an immigrant background.
AfD aims for opponents' destruction

Leading figures within the AfD have repeatedly described the CDU's "destruction" as a political objective. Torben Braga, a prominent lawyer, party strategist and AfD member of parliament, made the party's confrontational stance toward its political rivals clear during a panel discussion organized by the far-right publishing house Antaios.

According to Braga, the AfD's goal is to become strong enough either to govern on its own or to trigger such profound upheaval within competing parties that they are effectively transformed into entirely new political forces.
The AfD thus appears to be pinning its hopes on the CDU's gradual decline, focusing on attracting disillusioned conservative voters rather than working with the party.
Could the BSW become a coalition partner?

For the moment, that leaves only one realistic partner: the relatively new Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW). The party was founded by former Left Party star Sahra Wagenknecht, who has achieved electoral success with a left-wing economic platform and a foreign policy stance widely seen as sympathetic to Russia.

For the first time, the BSW has entered the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament and could now emerge as kingmaker for the AfD. The party has signaled its openness to talks and potential cooperation. The two parties also share significant common ground on policy.
Why MAGA supports Germany's rise of the far right

But shortly after its election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD also turned its fire on the BSW. Appearing on the far-right online channel Compact TV, AfD parliamentary group leader Oliver Kirchner referred to BSW politician Fabio De Masi as a "half-Italian." He went on to suggest that the BSW could not be relied upon if problems were ever to arise within a governing partnership.

The influential AfD leader in Thuringia, Björn Höcke, dismissed the BSW as the "latest cartel party." The signals coming from the AfD point neither to a willingness to compromise nor to any desire for rapprochement. On the contrary, even without a majority of its own, the party appears determined to stay the course and pursue its radical agenda.
AfD's national leadership wants to govern
But what if that still doesn't lead to an AfD-led government? "Then we'll simply have to hold another election. That's just how it is," Kirchner said on Compact TV.

That prospect, however, is unlikely to be welcomed by everyone within the party. "At the federal level, there is a strong interest in seeing the AfD lead the government in Saxony-Anhalt," observed political scientist Haussmann. Above all, the party's influential co-leader Weidel hopes to use an AfD-led state government as a stepping stone toward her long-term ambition of one day becoming chancellor.
Irregular migration 'a trigger point for radical parties'

DW also asked the AfD parliamentary group in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament, as well as a member of the party's state executive board, how the AfD is currently conducting coalition negotiations. Neither responded to a request for comment.

Despite its ongoing electoral successes, the AfD continues to face considerable internal tensions between its fundamentalist and pragmatic factions. Even if the party were to enter government through a coalition, public skepticism toward it in Germany would remain substantial.
"Even if the AfD were to succeed in forming a coalition with another party, that fact alone would not make it a more democratic party," said Haussmann
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches
articles.summary: Police reportedly fired into the air on Friday morning as they struggled to contain crowds jostling to secure a place at the tented site.

blocks.text: Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.
Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.
Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.
Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned, but it is believed that more than 13,000 remain in the enclave.
The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.
During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.

More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.
The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror had no doubt she deliberately killed her children
articles.summary: It is the first time the juror, who refused to side with the others and acquit Clancy, has spoken publicly about his decision.

blocks.text: The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children.

"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating.
Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated.
Warning: This article contains distressing details

The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window.

To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition.
The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder.
Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings.
"I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday.
"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented."
Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind.
"We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said.
The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster".

She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity."

Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side".
But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial.
The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations.
Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday.
In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began.
He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them".

During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis.
Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong.
A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children.

However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association.

Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility.
The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.
Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial.
He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy.
He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset."
The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

articles.title: New cat species identified for the 1st time in a century
articles.summary: A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia's cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described…

image.caption: A Leopardus tilcayo cat, a newly identified species through research led by National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, walks at the Senda Verde animal refuge in Bolivia's Yungas region on Sept. 1, 2026. (Fernando Faciole/National Geographic via Reuters)

blocks.text: Science·New

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia's cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.
Leopardus tilcayo is a tiger cat identified as a new species through genetic testing
The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is ‌part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America.

It was found in Bolivia's lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 46 centimetres (18 inches) long and weighs around three pounds, making it smaller than the average domestic cat.
Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, ​and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.

"Its fur is ​light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body," said Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.

Little is yet known about the cat's biology and ​lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be ⁠more active at night, Nogales Ascarrunz said.

Tiger ⁠cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, ‌said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart, of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.
Only 2 live individuals found so far
Referring to the new species, Lescroart said, "Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records."
One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives ⁠in Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.

Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because "its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats," Nogales Ascarrunz said. "This made us wonder: What tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?"
The team analyzed DNA from 38 cats sampled across ‌several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
"We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal — subspecies or otherwise," Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago.

"The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we ​estimate those lineages to have been physically separated," Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.

The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru's Yungas, naming it Leopardus ⁠tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca Empire that included the area it inhabits.
See some of the new species discovered in 2025
New species may be listed as endangered
The International Union for Conservation of Nature's red list, ⁠tracking the status of species, currently treats tiger cats as two "vulnerable" species with declining populations.

The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review ⁠will assess ⁠the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture ​of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could potentially be considered endangered when assessed on their own.
The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute ​in the Yungas, one of the region's most ⁠threatened ecosystems.

The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales Ascarrunz added.

"Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message," said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study.
"There are many undiscovered species out there ⁠in the world, and they are at risk of ‌disappearing before we even discover them."

articles.title: Manny Villar confident Ombudsman's graft claims over PrimeWater issue can be 'addressed'
articles.summary: Business tycoon Manny Villar, former Senate president and patriarch of the Villar Group of Companies, expressed confidence Friday that he and his family can dispute the graft charges leveled by the…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 7:40pm

Business tycoon Manny Villar, former Senate president and patriarch of the Villar Group of Companies, expressed confidence Friday that he and his family can dispute the graft charges leveled by the Office of the Ombudsman over the alleged poor service of their PrimeWater Infrastructure Corporation.

Villar, the ninth richest Filipino according to Forbes' 2026 list, issued the statement shortly after the Ombudsman announced that two counts of graft have been filed against him, his wife former senator Cynthia Villar, their senator-children Mark and Camille, and brother Paolo over the PrimeWater issue.

"We have learned through media reports of the complaints reportedly filed before the Office of the Ombudsman. As of this time, we have yet to receive copies of the complaints and therefore cannot meaningfully comment on their specific allegations," he said.

"We are confident that, once given the opportunity to examine the allegations and the evidence supporting them, we will be able to fully and properly defend our rights and address the matters raised against us," the Villar patriarch said.
Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said the Ombudsman's investigation lasted about six months, covering PrimeWater's joint venture deals with various water districts from 2015 to 2022.
Officials of several water districts are also included as respondents in the complaint.
The Villar family members, Clavano said, were the beneficial owners of PrimeWater during the period of investigation.
In December 2025, the Villar Group sold PWIC to Lucio Co Group’s Crystal Bridges Holding Corp.
The former Senate president assured that they will handle the matter in adherence to the law.
"We respect the legal process and will respond to the complaints at the appropriate time and in the proper forum," he added.
He also advised against prejudging the issues without giving those concerned a fair shake.
"We ask that the legal process be allowed to take its course and that conclusions not be drawn before the parties have been afforded the opportunity to be heard," he added.

Clavano cited alleged violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act related to government officials and individuals giving undue injury or unwarranted benefits, and for entering into disadvantageous public contracts.

Senator Mark served as the secretary of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) from 2016 to 2021 before launching a successful senatorial bid in 2022. The Local Water Utilities Administration, which regulates the local water districts, is an attached agency of the DPWH.
Mark, his sister Camille, their parents Manny and Cynthia, all served as representative of Las Piñas City ahead of their tenures in the Senate. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: At least 16 killed after vehicle loaded with explosives rams into Pakistan mosque
articles.summary: A vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque building during Friday prayers, a senior police official says.

blocks.text: At least 16 people, including five police officers, have been killed after a vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque in north-western Pakistan, according to a senior police official in Peshawar.
A gun battle is still ongoing between attackers and security forces at the mosque, near police headquarters, in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
One of the assailants has reportedly been killed, an officer says, and a rescue operation is under way.
In a statement, Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion."
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police chief inspector general Zulfikar Hameed described the attack as a "suicide attack" to Reuters news agency.
There has been no immediate claim of responsibility.
Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif also condemned the blast.
Militancy in Pakistan's border areas has risen sharply in recent months, targeting the military and police.
Islamabad says the militants use safe haven in Afghanistan to train and plan attacks in Pakistan.
Afghanistan's Taliban government has denied the accusation and said militancy is Pakistan's domestic problem.

articles.title: DFA urges delay in implementing P1.5K passport fee until 2028
articles.summary: The printing agency responsible for producing Philippine passports is seeking a price increase, but Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Theresa Lazaro said the agency has been asked to…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 7:36pm

The printing agency responsible for producing Philippine passports is seeking a price increase, but Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Theresa Lazaro said the agency has been asked to defer the proposed hike until 2028.
Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito said that the APO Production Unit, Inc. has reached out to him with their concern.

“They are saying that if they fail to adjust the price, they might be forced to cease their operations and baka mamaya, wala tayong passport by next year… siyempre this will be a big problem,” Ejercito said, citing a letter from the APO Production Unit.

(They are saying that if they fail to adjust the price, they might be forced to cease their operations and maybe soon, we will not have a passport by next year… of course, this will be a big problem.)

Ejercito said that the printing agency is asking for passport prices to be raised from P950 to P1,500. However, there will be discounted rates of P1,200 for senior citizens and overseas Filipino workers.

“Ito pong sulat ng APO is a consequence of certain negotiations. Nung sinabi nila na gusto nilang iakyat ang halaga ng passport from the present P950 to P1,500, ang sabi namin sa kanila, kung puwede niyo i-postpone muna yung pag-increase,” Lazaro said in response.

(This letter from APO is a consequence of certain negotiations. When they said that they want to increase the price of the passport from the present P950 to P1,500, we told them that, if it is possible, to postpone the increase.)
Lazaro said that the request was reasonable, since the last increase was more than 10 years ago. Adding to this was the extension of the passport’s validity from five years to 10 years.
However, Lazaro said that they asked APO to defer this increase since there will be a next-generation passport, which will be launched in the middle of 2028.
“You cannot increase the price of a passport within three years,” Lazaro said, citing the Philippine Passport Act.

Lazaro said that if they increased prices by January as per APO’s request, it may affect the planned next-generation passport. She also said that the DFA would need to make a communications plan for a passport price hike.
Ejercito said that the DFA should let the Senate know if there is a need to subsidize the passports, but admitted that there was a tight fiscal space. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootout
articles.summary:
Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police…

blocks.text: A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.

Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.

Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.

A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.
Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.

Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”
Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.
The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.

In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.

“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”

Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.
Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”
Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.
Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

articles.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
articles.summary: The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation infrastructure.

image.caption: Germany's shift to EVs is reducing emissions while eroding fuel tax revenues, raising questions about future transportation fundingImage: DW

blocks.text: "People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," said Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW).
"The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway," he told DW.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of this year compared to the same period last year.
Norway is leading the way, with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered passenger cars in the country.

The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was around 75%.
Fossil fuels remain a tax windfall

In Berlin, however, the boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm. That's particularly the case at the Ministry of Finance, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes.
Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 cents, and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax.
With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club.

The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, said Boysen-Hogrefe. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite."
Energy tax revenue in decline

"If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," the tax expert underscored, predicting billions of euros in losses.
EU overturns combustion engine ban amid industry pressure
According to the Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion ($43 billion) in 2016 to €33 billion ($38 billion) last year.
In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050.
Pressure to reform road funding

"The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report states. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, it added.
In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023.
However, electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits.
In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act.
That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued.
Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said.
How other countries are responding
Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures such as introducing new taxes.

In the UK, for instance, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids.
Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees.
Why big automakers are losing China

And in Switzerland, electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations.

Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles, has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls.
Are road tolls the answer?
In Germany, too, many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account.
"The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published study by the University of Münster.
"If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report.
Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period.
"If this, too, encounters insurmountable political resistance, the only solution left is to raise the motor vehicle tax," they concluded.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Early voting begins in midterms as campaign shifts focus to cost of living and Iran war – US politics live
articles.summary:
Campaigning or control of Congress is expected to ramp up as some states open early voting

Good morning, and welcome to our US politics live blog. The midterm elections are less than…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 18s agoTrump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
20m agoEarly voting begins in midterms as cost of living and Iran war loom large

blocks.text: Trump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
Alexandra Villarreal

The Trump administration has started sending a majority of undocumented children who came to the US alone and have new immigration court cases to Texas, where government facilities for them are unlicensed, their chances of getting a lawyer are low and advocates fear that “a deportation churn-out factory” awaits them, the Guardian has learned.

blocks.caption: Unaccompanied minors wait in Texas to be transported by the US Border Patrol after crossing the Rio Grande River from Mexico. Photograph: Go Nakamura/Reuters

blocks.text: Almost 80% of children in federal custody who arrived unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian and who were placed in immigration court proceedings in July – and over 90% in August – have been funneled into shelter networks somewhere in Texas, a dramatic upswing from the months prior, according to analysis shared exclusively with the Guardian from researchers at the immigration data insights platform bklg.org.

This is understood to amount to a total of 925 children in the care of the Health and Human Services (HHS) department’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR) and in open immigration court proceedings based in Texas, with 651 sent there in July and August alone.
Early voting begins in midterms as cost of living and Iran war loom large

Good morning, and welcome to our US politics live blog. The midterm elections are less than two months away, but some states begin early voting today, marking the start of a crucial stretch of campaigning for control of Congress.

Virginia begins early in-person voting, while voters in Minnesota, Idaho and South Dakota can cast absentee ballots in person, as the campaign turns increasingly on the cost of living and the continuing war in Iran.

blocks.caption: The start of early voting comes at a time of deep angst among many US citizens about issues including rising gas. Photograph: Nam Y Huh/AP

blocks.text: High gas prices and low approval ratings are adding to the challenges facing president Donald Trump as Republicans head into the 3 November elections with their control of the House and Senate at risk. In its analysis of the US economy, the Wall Street Journal reports that mortgage rates are nearing 7%, consumer prices rose 3.4% in the year to August and gas prices are close to their highest levels since 2022.

“We are seeing what happens when a president launches a war of choice without anticipating the unintended consequences,” Aaron David Miller, a former adviser on Middle East policy to Republican and Democratic administrations, told Reuters.

Trump will take his case to the UN on Tuesday, where he is likely to present the Iran war as a victory despite having initially promised the military campaign would be over within weeks. The conflict has instead entered its seventh month, with Iran still able to disrupt regional shipping and the war putting further pressure on global energy prices.
In other developments:

items: The Trump administration has approved a potential sale of 48 advanced F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, worth an estimated $24.3b. The Department of State said the propose sale “will improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense”. The move comes despite concerns from intelligence agencies that China could potentially gain access to, or steal, sensitive F-35 technology through Saudi Arabia, according to the New York Times. The newspaper reported:

blocks.text: double quotation markOne detailed report, issued months ago by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency, raised questions about whether the Americans and Saudis would be able to secure sites with F-35 technology. It also raised concerns about the access that Chinese military personnel have to Saudi bases and the prevalent use by Saudi Arabia of Chinese technology in telecommunications infrastructure and defense installations.

items: Former staff members of the US Institute of Peace have asked a federal appeals court to prevent the Trump administration from carving the president’s name into the facade of its headquarters in Washington, which was renamed the ‘“Donald J. Trump United States Institute of Peace” last year. Lawyers for the institute’s ousted board members argued that engraving Trump’s name on the building would cause “irreparable harm” by undermining the organization’s independent mission.

The USIP dispute comes as another Washington cultural institution faces a court battle over changes under Trump. A federal judge has ordered the Kennedy Center to give 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition as Trump has threatened. The president said the centre could be “ripped down” amid a dispute over plans to put his name on the building and a proposed $257m renovation. The center is currently closed due to what its Trump-backed leadership described as safety issues caused by age and structural deficiencies.

blocks.caption: Traffic cones keep cars from entering the driveway at the Kennedy Center in Washington, which was ordered to be closed for repairs by its board. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

articles.title: Dozens of suspected illegal miners die in Nigerian custody
articles.summary: Authorities linked the deaths to disease, but this has been disputed by intelligence reports and relatives of the accused.
articles.byline: Makuochi Okafor, Harry Sekulich, Wycliffe Muia

blocks.text: Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria have died in custody, local officials said.
Police have set up an investigation into the deaths, which the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) blamed on an apparent disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report shared with AFP news agency suggested the group died because of overcrowding and poor ventilation inside the detention facility in Niger state.
"We believe they suffocated because there was no ventilation," the father of one of those detained told the BBC.
Abdullahi Dalhatu said his son had survived because he was near a small window.
"His friend slumped and fainted, and many others also collapsed."
His son described how detainees began collapsing in the heat of the overcrowded and poorly ventilated cell, his father said.
He said the detainees repeatedly knocked on the door for help but nobody opened it.
State governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called the deaths "sad and tragic" during a press conference on Thursday.
An NSCDC commander has been detained following the deaths, Bago added.
He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections scheduled for January.
Officials had arrested the group of young men on Tuesday for suspected illegal mining near Borgu, in the mineral-rich state of Niger. The region is known for small-scale gold mining.

Two days later, 37 people detained as part of the suspected unlawful operation were found dead inside the detention centre run by the NSCDC, a paramilitary agency responsible for protecting critical infrastructure and tackling crimes including illegal mining. It also assists police with internal security operations.
The NSCDC told the BBC that illegal mining was widespread in Niger state, where artisanal miners often operate in open fields.

Its spokesperson, Babawale Afolabi, said more than 50 people were arrested during an operation earlier this week. They had not been charged because profiling and documentation were still under way before the deaths, he said.
"Illegal mining in Niger is serious," Afolabi said.
The NSCDC had earlier said the detainees were possibly victims of a diphtheria outbreak, a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal.
But the agency's national headquarters later said the cause had not been established and would require medical and laboratory tests.
"The NSCDC wishes to clarify that reports attributing the deaths to any specific disease remain subject to medical and laboratory confirmation," it added in a statement.
Dalhatu told the BBC that security officers had been pursuing suspected illegal miners in the community for several days before making arrests.
He said relatives went to the NSCDC office seeking their release but were repeatedly told to return later. "Unfortunately, the following day we got the news that our children had died," he added.
One father told Nigerian media that his son had appeared healthy when relatives took him food the day before his death and called for an independent post-mortem examination.

Another relative, whose 17-year-old brother was among those who died, said the family had visited him during his detention and questioned how a disease could have killed so many detainees without apparently affecting their guards.
Post-mortem examinations are expected to help establish what happened.

Niger's police chief ordered an immediate investigation into "the unfortunate death of suspected illegal miners while in the detention facility of the NSCDC", spokesman Wasiu Abiodun wrote in a statement.
The victim's bodies have since been taken to the general hospital in nearby Minna for examination.
It is not clear yet whether any of the suspects had been charged.

Nigeria's constitution requires anyone detained on suspicion of a criminal offence to be brought before a court within a "reasonable time" - generally within a day where a court is available within 40km (25 miles), or two days in other cases, unless a longer period is considered reasonable.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state has been blamed for fuelling criminal gang violence, according to officials and experts.
Much of the gold in the region is trafficked through global supply chains, a 2024 SwissAid report found.

articles.title: Women's football in Germany booming but still much to do
articles.summary: Women's football is growing rapidly, particularly in Germany. Nevertheless, equal pay and investment remain major talking points.

image.caption: Women's football in Germany has made strides in recent years, but still has work to do to improve its professional structuresImage: Grant Hubbs/STEINSIEK.CH/IMAGO

blocks.text: According to the German Football Association (DFB), investment in women's football by professional clubs has risen by 135% over the past six years. In addition, the number of girls in Germany who play the game has increased by about 30% since 2022.
Celia Sasic, the former Germany striker who has been in charge of diversity and inclusion at the DFB since 2022, has helped bring women's football more into the spotlight in the boardroom.
"We've focused on the issue and established new structures, so that there is now a separate department with its own sports director," the 38-year-old told DW.
"In my view, it's important that there are very clear responsibilities for the development and professionalization of this sport."

"I believe it's important that [women's football] is recognized within the licensed clubs. And it's becoming increasingly recognized, so the framework conditions need to be adjusted," continued Sasic.
"And we're seeing that if we provide the right framework for the game, there's huge growth potential there."

blocks.caption: Celia Sasic has been fighting for equality in women's football for years and wants better structures in the women's game in GermanyImage: Simon Hofmann/Getty Images

blocks.text: Numbers support growth of women's game

The most-watched football match featuring a German team in 2025 was the Women's European Championship semifinal between Germany and Spain. The match drew around 14.26 million viewers—and a market share of about 57.6%. By comparison, the men's game against Portugal in the Nations League semifinals drew around 10 million viewers.
Sasic, who was part of the German team that won the 2009 and 2013 European championships, regards this as a foundation to build on.
"This is incredibly significant for us as a society and in terms of our influence abroad," she said.
"There are women who play football, who play for us on the national team, and who inspire us so much that millions of us watch their games."
'Zidane was my hero'
Sasic is clearly proud of the recent progress. For a long time, women's football in Germany was not taken seriously.
"I had no choice; I had to look to men for role models," Sasic recalled.
"My biggest role model was Zinedine Zidane. I had posters of [Luis] Figo, [David] Beckham, and Michael Ballack hanging in my room."

Posters of women wouldn't have existed back then, but it's different now. These days, Germany captain Giulia Gwinn and players like Jule Brandt and Lea Schüller smile down from the walls of children's bedrooms, inspiring girls to dream of a great career in women's football.

blocks.caption: Support of the women's team has exploded in recent years in GermanyImage: Eddie Keogh/Getty Images

blocks.text: Further investment required to push women's game forward

Despite the boom, the financial gap between women's and men's football remains enormous, as figures from the DFB and the German Soccer League (DFL) show. While the 18 Bundesliga clubs spent €1.72 billion ($1.9 billion) on players and coaching staff alone in the 2024–25 season, the personnel expenses of the 12 Women's Bundesliga clubs most recently totaled just under €30 million — about 60 times lower.

Salaries also highlight how the professionalization of women's football is still very much in its infancy. In the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year. Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is estimated to have earned €25 million during the same season.
This disparity is expected to narrow in the future.
"Football reflects our society—and thus also the gender inequality and the gender pay gap that we see in our society," former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock told DW.

"Unfortunately, this gap in football is even wider in many countries than in other professions. But that is by no means set in stone," added Baerbock, who also served as the president of the United Nations General Assembly from September 2025 to September 2026.

"We know from the USA, the United Kingdom, Norway, and Spain that if you really want to invest in women's football, equal pay is an important part of that—especially when it comes to tournament bonuses."

blocks.caption: Annalena Baerbock believes change in terms of equal pay lies in the hands of football nationsImage: Eduardo Munoz/REUTERS

blocks.text: Young women need professional support
Celia Sasic currently sees significant progress when it comes to women's football, although it's still early days in the development process.

"Clubs must provide all the necessary resources to enable this development. Football pitches, medical care, a fitness facility, and a coaching staff must be available," said Sasic. "Investing in this ultimately makes the game much better, too."
Opportunities for young girls in terms of training also need to improve.
"It's a crucial step to have youth development centers where players are trained—not only athletically, but also professionally. These are essential factors for the success of the women's game."

blocks.caption: Bayern Munich offer some of the best training facilities in the country, but the aim is to improve all the facilities in GermanyImage: Jenni Maul/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Education and apprenticeship options must be available

A new DFB rule shows that even basic professional structures still need to be established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches, and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

Sasic and women's football still have a long way to go, but the former player is determined to continue fighting for greater equality. The 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil is a great place to start, and Sasic is hoping for a successful showing for Germany at the tournament as this would likely give women's football another major boost—and bring broadcasters new record viewership ratings.
This article was adapted from German.
